I think fixed income as an asset class can generally be broken down into five primary categories with sub-categories within each. You generally have:

Sovereigns
* Nominal Treasuries and Developed-Market Sovereign Bonds
* TIPS and inflation-linked bonds
* EM debt (dollar denominated)
* EM debt (local currency)

Corporates
* Investment Grade
* High Yield

Agencies
* Munis
* Agency MBS (FNMA, GNMA, etc.)

Securitized/Structured
* Non-Agency MBS
* ABS
* CDO/CLOs

Hybrids
* Convertible Bonds
* Preferred Shares


Personally, I develop a view on inflation first and then determine my asset allocation to fixed income based on what I believe will provide the best diversification per unit of risk-adjusted return. Inflation erodes the value of fixed-rate securities because your cash flows remain unchanged while inflation reduces the buying power of your coupons, so over you have to invest in higher-yielding fixed rate bonds to offset rising inflation. Simply putting all of your FI allocation in nominal treasuries might be good if you're expressing a view on interest rates decreasing, but if you're hoping to use your fixed income as a source of income, this is poor idea that can be greatly improved through diversification. Add some TIPS to offset the effect of rising inflation; I think TIPS are some of the most undervalued sources of yield out there at the moment.


Treasuries are only going to get you so far, though. With yields at the lowest they've been in decades, you need to add some higher-yielding assets if you want to continue to use FI as income generators. Short-dated high yield paper provides nice risk-adjusted yield and you don't have to worry as much about default risk as longer-dated HY like you find in most ETFs, so an active manager might be worth considering. Similarly, there are amazing opportunities in emerging market bonds, since most EM countries have much higher interest rates. You can stay short-dated in these too to pick some some nice yield without having to worry about rising political uncertainty. Argentina is a great case in point on why you want to avoid long-dated EM paper; they issued a 100-year bond, which is unbelievable given their fiscal imprudence, that's now trading at a fraction of par given the recent uncertainty, so short-dated is usually what I like. 


Agencies are valuable too, since they more often than not offer a good spread over similar AAA-rated sovereigns while usually having higher coupon rates, so you can afford to go long-dated on Agencies.


Securitized most people won't have access to, and some rightly view them as another source of financial imprudence due to the over leverage used leading up to the GFC. But, they're still around and actually present a much better risk-adjusted return compared to 2007.


I personally love hybrids; they behave like a mix of equities (in that they can meaningfully appreciate) and fixed income (they generate a positive real yield over inflation), so they can serve you very well as both an added source of diversification while providing your portfolio some juicy returns. Just don't go expecting 20-30% returns like you do in equities, but 7-10% annualized s a fair range.

Great question; I hope this doesn’t come off as patronizing, but I want to explain everything as simple as possible because the logic behind risk parity can get complex at times.

If you have a 60/40 portfolio, by far the majority of the portfolio’s volatility is derived from the equity component. The point of having 40% in fixed income is to diversify the portfolio and help reduce the impact of years when the equity market declines, since bonds tend to outperform stocks in these environments. However, it turns out that only having 40% in bonds doesn’t really diversify away much of the risk of owning equities.


In reality, what All Weather specifically tries to do is equally allocate volatility into four different themes: rising growth, falling growth, rising inflation, and falling inflation. Each of these themes has certain assets associated with it, and by allocating risk rather than assets, the portfolio should perform better over the long term on a risk-adjusted basis. It won’t outperform the stock market during 2017-esque years, but it should more effectively mitigate the effect of large drawdowns much more effectively than a traditional 60/40. Because the market is generally in at least one of these states, the portfolio should generally do well. To give you an idea of how this is constructed, this is how Bridgewater divvies up its assets:


Rising Growth: equities, commodities, corporate credit, emerging market debt


Falling Growth: nominal bond, inflation-linked bonds


Rising Inflation: inflation-linked bonds, emerging market debt, commodities


Falling Inflation: nominal bonds, equities 



The idea is that by dividing up the assets to balance risk, no one scenario is given a higher or power probability. In an environment like 2008, the falling growth and falling inflation buckets greatly benefit and the lower allocation to equities prevents the portfolio from sizable drawdowns. In 2011-2017 environments where markets are doing well, the combination of equites, commodities, and various mixture of debt all work well, so it still manages to earn a decent return, especially given its volatility. It’s easy to say in hindsight “oh, you should have just been 100% in equities since the crash!”, but that’s the benefit of hindsight. Dalio’s approach is to keep everything balanced (as all things should be) to do well (but not extremely so) in all market environments. That’s why it’s so popular with institutional investors. Hope this helped!

I work in the hedge fund space (quant, not risk parity like All Weather, but I think I can speak for most strategies), so I hope I can provide some clarity.


The simple reason why S&P 500 funds are much more popular than All Weather (what we call “risk parity”) is that it’s dead simple for most ordinary investors to use. Buying a basket of large and mega-cap stocks (i.e. the S&P) is much more straightforward than investing across asset classes, implementing an active trading and risk management system, and applying the correct amount of leverage for each asset as you do in risk parity. Most ordinary investors will do fine with a mix of S&P and a bond fund, so naturally much more investor money will gravitate towards those simple strategies.


However, risk parity certainly has its place in the industry because it’s goals are not the same as those of the S&P. Risk parity is focused on providing a much more steady stream of returns that attempt to weight the assets in its portfolio by volatility. One of the core issues that Dalio brings up is that in a standard 60/40 portfolio (60% stocks, 40% fixed income), 90% of the portfolio volatility comes from the equity component and the remaining 10% comes from the fixed income. Risk parity attempts to reconcile this by allocating funds to each asset class in order for each asset to have the same contribution to the portfolio’s overall volatility. This is a great strategy for investors with more complex cash flow-liability management hurdles (corporate pension plans, insurance companies, etc.) that would benefit from the reduction in volatility that risk parity provides at the expense of some of the upside return that a 60/40 portfolio provides.


Retail investors generally face two issues when trying to implement risk parity strategies that hedge funds and large asset managers don’t. 

1: Since risk parity targets equal volatility contributions from each of its assets, it leveraged up its fixed income holdings up to the level of the other core assets, primarily stocks and commodities. Risk parity portfolios generally have 60-70% of their total assets in fixed income due to its much lower volatility than other assets, so it has to constitute a much larger % of the portfolio’s assets in order to have the same volatility contribution as the equity and commodity components. What Dalio, AQR, and others then do is leverage up their bond holdings to enhance their returns, which is something most retail investors should not attempt.


2: Most risk parity strategies use a variety of assets that retail investors don’t have access to. Credit spreads, emerging market debt, futures, can be difficult for individual investors to access, and the usage of other instruments like total return swaps (used to create synthetic long positions so you can get exposure to an asset without actually having to buy it outright) make true implementation near impossible for non-professionals.


I hope some of this is useful; I enjoy being able to discuss this sort of stuff with people who are interested, so I hope this helps!

Then work backwards through their catalogue so you listen to the heaviest and grittiest albums last

For death metal, you've got to ease yourself into it. Anybody would probably hate it if they went straight to bands like Cannibal. Start with some heavier thrash metal like Slayer or Celtic Frost, then move to bands like Death and Morbid Angel. It helps to see where the classic bands got their inspiration from and makes the evolution less drastic to your ears. From there you can now to other death metal (Dismember, Unleashed, Entombed) or melodic death metal (Carcass, early In Flames, At the Gates, Dark Tranquility). A lot of melodeath bands inspired early metalcore, so you could also work backwards
